name: Hallstatt culture
title: The story of the Hallstatt culture

text: More than 3,000 years ago, the Hallstatt culture grew up in Europe, around the Alps.
It is named after Hallstatt, a lakeside village in Austria with a salt mine.
src: c. 1200 BCE: The finds at Hallstatt begin / Western and central Europe / the settlements north of the Alps / In northern Italy the Golasecca culture, an early western example of the Hallstatt movement
The Hallstatt culture takes its name from Hallstatt, a lakeside village in the Austrian Salzkammergut south-east of Salzburg, with a rich salt mine

text: Its people worked bronze, and about 2,800 years ago they began making iron too.
Most were farmers in small villages, but at Hallstatt, digging salt made people rich.
src: Hallstatt A (1200–1050 BCE) and B (1050–800 BCE), the Late Bronze Age Urnfield culture / c. 800 BCE: Iron ore processing arrives

Hallstatt society was based on farming / Most settlements were small villages / The salt mines of Hallstatt, worked most intensively from the 8th to the 5th centuries BCE, made its community unusually rich

text: Chiefs lived in forts on hilltops, where smiths worked bronze, silver and gold.
src: The largest were mostly fortified hilltop sites, often with the workshops of bronze, silver and gold smiths / emerging elites of chieftains and warriors

text: From Greeks and Etruscans in the south came amber, ivory, fine pots and probably wine.
A Celtic city named by the Greek writer Herodotus may be one of their forts, the Heuneburg.
src: traded with the Greek and Etruscan Mediterranean / Amber, ivory, as in the Grafenbühl tomb, red kermes dye, found at Hochdorf, and probably wine came north / Attic black-figure pottery in elite graves attests trade with Greece
The Heuneburg on the upper Danube, ringed by nine very large grave mounds, is thought to be the Celtic city of Pyrene mentioned by Herodotus

text: Great chiefs were buried under big earth mounds, with wagons and rich goods.
A grave at Hochdorf held a bronze couch carried by little figures on single wheels.
src: high-status people were buried under large mounds near fortified hilltop settlements, in timber-lined chambers with the body and the grave goods set about the room. Some graves held a chariot or wagon
the bronze couch held up by “unicyclists” from the Hochdorf Chieftain’s Grave

text: About 2,400 years ago, their centres were destroyed or left, and the La Tène culture followed.
Salt has kept their cloth, wood and leather, and their treasures are now in museums.
src: c. 450 BCE: Hallstatt D gives way to the La Tène culture after great centres such as the Heuneburg are destroyed or abandoned
the salt has preserved cloth, wood, leather and tools / the Hallstatt Museum in the town holds the largest / German and Austrian museums
